prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, whose magic-wavelength trapping enabled timekeeping and frequency comparison at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a measurement advance of the kind I think limits what physics can do. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removed the light-shift problem that blocked trapped neutral atoms, and it allowed many atoms to be interrogated at once. Ye's group then took strontium lattice clocks to the 10^-18 regime in both systematic uncertainty and stability. The performance is documented in clock-to-clock comparisons within and between laboratories and over fibre links, which is the experimental evidence I trust most. It has opened new observables: gravitational redshift resolved over millimetres, searches for variation of fundamental constants and for dark matter, and relativistic geodesy. It is also the basis for the pending redefinition of the second. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: two names, one conceptual origin and one flagship realisation. Several independent groups (Sr, Yb, Hg) have reproduced and surpassed the early results, so maturity is not in doubt.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this field has already been recognised: Hall and Haensch in 2005 for laser precision spectroscopy and the comb, Wineland in 2012 for ion control and ion clocks. A committee could read lattice clocks as the next increment in precision rather than a new conceptual step. There is also a real priority question, because other groups (Lemonde at SYRTE, Takamoto and Katori, Ludlow and Bloom, Ye's colleagues at NIST and JILA) share parts of the achievement and a two-name prize leaves them out. Finally, B046 and B028 have broader support from colleagues and arguably a larger footprint across physics. If the committee values field-opening impact over measurement capability, they could reasonably come first.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the lattice clock fifth. He values it as a precision-instrument achievement but notes overlap with Hall and Haensch (2005) and Wineland (2012), and that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened.
responses.response: I take the overlap seriously, but I think it is smaller than it looks. The comb is a ruler for optical frequencies and Wineland's work is single-ion control. The lattice clock solves a different problem: how to get the statistics of millions of atoms while removing the trapping perturbation. That is why it reached a stability that ion clocks could not reach in practical averaging times. That was a new idea, not an incremental step. On the redefinition, I agree with you that it does not affect the physics. The clock comparisons already deliver the measurement result, and a redefinition would add practical impact on top of it.

responses.point: Mehlig puts topological insulators first because of the simple, general Z2 mechanism and calls recognition overdue. He would take Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as the core and treats Hasan as a defensible alternative for 3D materials.
responses.response: I accept that the Kane-Mele idea is elegant and well confirmed, and I did not rank B028 in my own top eight, so I should explain why it is not in my first position. The credit problem is real: your own and Olle's openings both say that Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, who enabled the HgTe experiment, and the 3D strand with Hasan cannot all be honoured within three names. A prize that must leave out the theorists whose prediction made the HgTe experiment possible has an attribution weakness the lattice clock does not have. I would not oppose B028 as a second choice, which is why it is one of my alternatives, but I would want the 2D and 3D allocation settled before supporting it.

responses.point: Olsson ranks magic-angle graphene first and the lattice clock second. She argues for Jarillo-Herrero, MacDonald and Andrei, because Andrei's earlier STM evidence of flat bands is part of the record and Bistritzer would be left out.
responses.response: We agree that the clock is a strong candidate and I appreciate your note that the credited set is clean. On twisted bilayer graphene, I rank it second and the physics is striking. My hesitation is the one you and Olle raise: the superconducting mechanism is still debated and the field is only about eight years old. I would also push back gently on your choice of names. If the prize is for the 2018 correlated-insulator and superconductivity discovery, the theory prediction by Bistritzer and MacDonald is what made it a targeted experiment, so leaving Bistritzer out while including Andrei changes the logic of the citation. I think this attribution should be settled by checking priority carefully before that prize is proposed.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clock first for the same reasons of precision and fundamental tests. She sees little credit ambiguity and ranks optical-lattice quantum simulation (B011) second.
responses.response: I agree with your reading of the clock, and our shared view shows the kind of support the case has from atomic physics. Where I differ slightly is B011, which I rank fifth. The Hubbard-model simulation is scientifically deep, but your own opening says five credited names cannot all be honoured, and Jaksch is missing entirely. I also think a prize for the quantum simulator has to be argued on what it has produced that was not already known from solids, and that has still been less convincing to me than the clock comparisons. I would like to hear which result you consider decisive.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes to avoid the incremental-precision objection.

Whether Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Bloom or others have claims strong enough to alter the two-name configuration; my priority recollections come from memory and are not verified against the supplied text.
Whether the committee prefers to wait for the redefinition of the second, or considers the demonstrated performance enough.
Whether the flat-band and topological candidates are judged to outweigh a measurement-science prize on breadth of impact.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile. One minor connection to flag: I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder during my PhD, and Ye is a JILA colleague of Hall's lineage, but I have no direct collaboration with either candidate that would require recusal. I also have no links to the other shortlisted candidates. My WACQT leadership overlaps institutionally with Chalmers, where Goran Johansson works, but that bears on B035, which is not in my preferred configuration.
